issues.explanation: The profile only includes Memory and Negative Appraisals, with the formulation showing a strong reciprocal link specifically between these two nodes. The memory items are dominated by trauma-recall qualities and guilt on recall, but 'Body as Enemy' and especially the globally externalized appraisal 'Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you' shift toward current somatic threat/general danger beliefs that are not reflected in the memory content and are hard to reconcile with the otherwise memory-centred formulation. Given no active Threat or Trigger links, these appraisal items do not align well with the specified cognitive pattern.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: This appraisal is hard to reconcile with the provided cognitive formulation. The only active connections are between Negative Appraisals and Memory, suggesting appraisals should be closely tied to trauma recollection and meaning-making about the event. A generalized interpersonal-danger belief ('You can never know who will harm you') implies an active Threat focus, yet Threat is otherwise unrepresented and all Threat-related edges are inactive. The other appraisal items are self-blaming and memory-linked (weakness, inaction guilt), so this one pulls the profile toward a different formulation not supported elsewhere.

vignette:
Carlos was fifty-five years old, a career Navy officer who had spent decades moving between bases and deployments, proud of his composure under pressure. That composure had cracked on a Tuesday afternoon three years ago, in a market square in a city that had once been a rest-and-recreation stop for personnel. He had been off-duty, buying a birthday present for his partner, when the first mortar round hit the far end of the square. The blast was a wall of sound and dust and heat that knocked him sideways. He remembered scrambling to his feet, pieces of stone and glass cutting his hands, and then the second round came closer. By then the air smelled of burnt metal and sweet, coppery blood. He saw a woman crouched over a child—a boy maybe six or seven—whose leg was twisted and bleeding badly. Carlos had first-aid training. He ran toward them. A petty officer grabbed his arm and shouted that they had to get to cover, that it wasn’t safe. Carlos tried to pull free, but the man was bigger, and they were both running now, away. The last thing he saw before the dust swallowed everything was the boy’s face, mouth open, silent. Three civilians died that day. The boy survived, but Carlos never learned how badly he was damaged.

In the weeks afterward, the memory would ambush him without warning. He would be standing on the bridge during a routine watch, and suddenly the heat and the smell and the screaming were right there in the room with him, as real as the first moment. His heart would pound, his hands would go slick, and for a few seconds he could not tell where he was. At other times—usually late at night, lying beside his sleeping partner—he would deliberately run through the events as if trying to fix them in his mind, but he found he could do it without feeling anything. He could describe the boy’s face, the pattern of blood on the cobblestones, the weight of the petty officer’s hand on his arm, and it all felt distant, like a scene from a movie that had happened to a stranger. That numbness frightened him more than the flashbacks. He had come to believe that a real man, a good officer, would have felt something—would have done something. He had not. He had been pulled away, and he had let it happen. He was certain he was weak, fundamentally and unforgivably weak. He would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, for not protecting the people who needed him. He should have protected them. He had failed.

So he began to avoid the places and situations that might trigger the full reliving. He stopped going into the port cities near his base. He took a desk assignment, claiming he needed to focus on paperwork, and he stopped volunteering for the kind of expeditionary duties that had once defined his career. When his commanding officer offered him a temporary billet on a ship heading to a region with a recent conflict, Carlos made an excuse about his aging mother needing care. He knew it was a lie, and he hated himself for the lie, but the thought of being anywhere near a crowded civilian market or the sound of a sudden, loud bang made his throat close. His partner noticed that he had become quiet, that he no longer wanted to go out for dinner in the city, that he flinched at the pop of a car backfiring. When she asked what was wrong, he said he was tired. He did not tell her about the boy or the blood or the way he sometimes went numb. He was afraid that if he told her, she would see what he saw: a man who had failed, a man who could not protect anyone, a man who did not deserve to wear the uniform.

What finally brought him to the clinic was not a decision he made alone. During a routine emergency drill on base, a fire alarm triggered a series of loud, percussive blasts from a nearby training exercise. Carlos dropped to the deck, covered his head, and could not get up for nearly a minute. His commanding officer saw it. After the drill, the officer told him, gently, that he needed to see someone. Carlos agreed because he knew he would be grounded otherwise, and being grounded felt like a public confession of everything he believed about himself. He walked into the therapist’s office with his hands clenched at his sides, certain that the first thing the therapist would see was how weak he was. What he hoped for, though he could barely admit it even to himself, was that someone might show him how to stop the memories from overwhelming him—without forcing him to talk about what it meant that he had let that boy bleed.
